video.title: Share with care
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher, the student's teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor holds a phone; a voice-note bubble jumps from chat to chat across many class groups.
scenes.animation: The bubble multiplies across group icons.
scenes.narration: Last term, a voice note reached every class group in our school. It said exams were cancelled. It sounded exactly like our head teacher, but it wasn't him.

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.narration: Today: how to share with care, from friends' photos to fakes made to fool you.

scenes.visual: Two friends; one holds up a phone with a photo of the other, who raises a hand: wait.
scenes.animation: A speech bubble 'Can I post this?' pops up, then 'No, please'.
scenes.narration: Start with people. A photo of your friend is part of their footprint, not yours. So before you post it, ask. If they say no, that's the answer, and even a funny photo can hurt when the whole school sees it.

scenes.visual: Three crossed-out cards: a private photo, a screenshot of a private chat, a phone filming someone being pushed.
scenes.animation: A red cross stamps each card.
scenes.narration: Some things are never shared: private or embarrassing pictures of someone else, screenshots of a private chat, or a video of someone being hurt. Sharing them can be bullying. Sharing private images of anyone under eighteen can also be a crime, even if they sent them to you.

scenes.visual: Three posts with a magnifying glass: an old flood photo with today's date, an edited picture, a waveform labelled AI.
scenes.animation: The magnifier slides over each in turn.
scenes.narration: Now, fakes. Some posts are made to fool you: an old photo with a new story, an edited picture, or a voice or video made with AI. They spread fast because they make us feel something strong.

scenes.visual: A fire alarm rings above a phone showing an angry face; a thumb stops just before the Share button.
scenes.animation: The alarm shakes; the thumb freezes.
scenes.on_screen_text: A strong feeling is an alarm
scenes.narration: A strong feeling works like a fire alarm. When a post makes you angry, scared or very excited, the alarm is ringing. That's exactly the moment to pause, before your thumb taps Share.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor shows a post from an unknown account: 'School closed tomorrow!'
scenes.narration: Quick check! A shocking post from an account you don't know says school is closed tomorrow. What do you do first?

scenes.visual: The 'check the official channel' card gets the check badge; the school's page opens beside it.
scenes.narration: Check the school's official channel: its page, its group, or a teacher. A stranger's account can't prove itself.

scenes.visual: A checklist appears beside a post; four boxes tick one after another.
scenes.animation: Each box ticks as it is named.
scenes.narration: Before you share, run four checks. Who made it? Is it new, or an old story? Do trusted sources say the same? And is it trying to make me angry or scared?

scenes.visual: A student sees a mean post about a classmate; she sends the classmate a kind message, taps Report, and talks to a teacher.
scenes.animation: Three panels appear one after another.
scenes.narration: If you see someone being bullied online, you can help. Don't forward it, and don't add a laughing face. Send the person a kind message. Keep a screenshot of the mean messages, report the post, and tell an adult you trust.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor shows a chat: a friend sends a funny photo of a classmate asleep at his desk.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A friend sends you a funny photo of a classmate asleep in class. Do you share it in the class group?

scenes.visual: The 'not without asking' card gets the check badge, then four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: Not without asking him, because it's his photo and his choice. Remember: ask before you post, never share private images, pause when you feel something strong, and check before you share.

scenes.visual: A student's phone shows a viral post; a ten-minute timer runs while she checks the official page.
scenes.animation: The timer counts down; a check mark appears.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: the next time a shocking post reaches you, wait ten minutes before you share anything. Run the four checks, and tell a friend what you found.

checkpoints.prompt: A shocking post from an account you don't know says school is closed tomorrow. What do you do first?

options.text: Share it fast so friends know
Ask the account if it's true

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the school's own page, group or a teacher can tell you. A stranger's account can't prove itself.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — sharing spreads a rumour, and the account that posted it will just say yes. Check the school's official channel.

checkpoints.prompt: A friend sends you a funny photo of a classmate asleep in class. Do you share it in the class group?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it's his photo and his choice. A joke stops being funny when the whole school is laughing at you.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a photo of someone is part of their footprint. Ask him first, and respect a no.
